slides.title: What statistics gives you for ML
slides.body:
Statistics is the discipline of turning data into claims. For ML researchers, the relevant statistics aren't the textbook hypothesis tests — they're a specific subset:

- **Estimation theory**: how to fit a distribution to data. MLE, MAP, Bayesian inference.
- **Hypothesis testing**: when can we say model A is better than model B?
- **Calibration**: when the model says '90% probability,' is it right 90% of the time?
- **Uncertainty quantification**: how confident should we be in a model's prediction?
- **The base-rate problem**: why benchmark accuracy can mislead.

This lesson is the applied version — estimation, testing, and the failure modes you actually encounter when evaluating models.

slides.title: Maximum likelihood estimation
slides.body:
Given data `D = {x_1, x_2, ...}` and a parametric model `p(x | θ)`, **MLE** finds the parameters that make the data most probable:

$$\hat{\theta}_{MLE} = \arg\max_\theta \prod_i p(x_i | \theta) = \arg\max_\theta \sum_i \log p(x_i | \theta)$$

The log is just for numerical stability — the product of many probabilities underflows; the sum of log-probabilities doesn't.

MLE is what training a neural net does. The cross-entropy loss is `-log p(y | x; θ)` summed over training examples. Gradient descent on this loss = MLE.

Properties:
- **Consistent**: as data → ∞, MLE → true parameters (under regularity conditions).
- **Asymptotically efficient**: lowest possible variance among consistent estimators.
- **NOT unbiased in general**: MLE for variance underestimates by a known factor.
- **Sensitive to model misspecification**: if the parametric family doesn't include the truth, MLE finds the closest member of the family — which might be far from truth.

slides.title: Hypothesis testing for model comparison
slides.body:
You trained model A and model B. A scores 0.873 on the test set; B scores 0.881. Is B actually better, or is the difference noise?

The right question isn't 'is the difference real' — it's 'how often would I see a difference this large if both models were equally good?' That's a p-value.

For classification accuracy: paired bootstrap test. Resample test examples with replacement; compute the difference in accuracy on each resample; the distribution of differences gives you a confidence interval.

For language model perplexity / loss: same idea, paired over tokens (or, more honestly, over evaluation examples).

**Critical**: the bootstrap test only validates that the difference is statistically significant. It doesn't tell you the difference is **practically meaningful** or that B will outperform A on a different dataset (generalization gap).

Most ML benchmark papers don't report confidence intervals. This is a problem. A 0.5% accuracy difference is often within bootstrap CI of zero — meaning the headline 'A beats B' is statistically indistinguishable from 'A and B are equivalent.'

question.question: Model A scores 0.872 on a 10K-example test set. Model B scores 0.880 on the same set. Which is more likely to indicate a real difference in capability?
options: B is clearly better — 0.8% accuracy difference
Hard to say without knowing the variance — a 0.8% difference on 10K examples could easily be within the bootstrap confidence interval of zero
B is clearly better, but you'd want more decimals
A is better because it's more conservative
question.explanation: On 10K examples, the standard error of accuracy is roughly √(p(1-p)/n) ≈ √(0.13/10000) ≈ 0.0036. A 0.8% (0.008) difference is about 2 standard errors — borderline statistically significant on a paired test, but barely. Most ML papers don't report this; the field's headline numbers often overstate the gap between models.

slides.title: Calibration
slides.body:
A model is **calibrated** if its predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. When the model says '90%,' the prediction should be right 90% of the time.

Calibration is NOT the same as accuracy:
- A model can be 100% accurate but uncalibrated (always says 60% confidence, but is right 100% of the time).
- A model can be 60% accurate and calibrated (says 60% confidence, right 60% of the time).

Why this matters: if the model's confidence is wrong, downstream decisions based on the confidence are wrong. Risk-weighted decisions, abstention thresholds, ensembling — all assume calibration.

Measure with a **reliability diagram**: bin predictions by their confidence; plot mean confidence vs accuracy in each bin. A perfectly calibrated model produces the diagonal y=x line. **Expected Calibration Error (ECE)** is the bin-weighted average distance from the diagonal.

Neural networks tend to be **overconfident**: they say 99% when they're 80% accurate. Temperature scaling (post-hoc calibration: divide logits by a learned temperature) is the cheapest fix. More principled approaches exist but are rarely used in production.

slides.title: The base-rate fallacy
slides.body:
A medical test has 99% sensitivity (true positive rate) and 95% specificity (true negative rate). A patient tests positive. What's the probability they have the disease?

Depends on the **base rate**. If the disease affects 1 in 10,000 people:

- Prior: P(disease) = 0.0001
- P(positive | disease) = 0.99
- P(positive | no disease) = 0.05
- P(positive) ≈ 0.05 (dominated by the false positive rate × no-disease population)
- P(disease | positive) = 0.99 × 0.0001 / 0.05 ≈ 0.002 = 0.2%

**A 99% sensitive test with a 5% false-positive rate, applied to a rare condition, gives 0.2% probability of disease given positive.** The headline number 'sensitivity is 99%!' is meaningless without the base rate.

This comes up constantly in ML evaluation:

- A spam classifier with 99% accuracy is great if 50% of email is spam, useless if 0.1% is.
- A medical diagnosis model is misleading without the prevalence.
- A safety classifier on rare adversarial inputs has its precision dominated by the false-positive rate, not the model's quality on the positive class.

The lesson: **always know the base rate**. Conditional probability is asymmetric (`P(disease | positive) ≠ P(positive | disease)`). One of the most consistent confusions in applied statistics.

question.question: What's a model that's 'calibrated but inaccurate'?
options: A model that says '60% confidence' on inputs where it's right 60% of the time. The confidence is well-tuned even though raw accuracy is low
A model with no probability outputs
A model trained for too long
question.explanation: Calibration is about confidence matching frequency. A model that's 60% accurate but reliably reports 60% confidence is calibrated. Calibration and accuracy are independent axes of model quality — both matter, neither implies the other.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
Statistics is the discipline of being honest with data. ML papers without confidence intervals, calibration, and base-rate awareness are doing it wrong.

Key takeaways:
- MLE is what training does. Cross-entropy minimization = MLE.
- A 0.5-1% difference in accuracy on a benchmark is often statistically indistinguishable from noise. Confidence intervals matter.
- Calibration ≠ accuracy. A model can be one without the other.
- Base rates flip the answer. P(disease | positive) ≠ P(positive | disease) in general.
